bib.title: Secrets of RLHF in Large Language Models Part I: PPO

question: Why is PPO-based RLHF unstable for LLMs, which components of PPO matter, and what stable recipe (PPO-max) can be given?
hypothesis: Policy constraints are the key factor for stable PPO in RLHF, and a carefully chosen combination of tricks avoids pattern collapse.
contributions: Release competitive Chinese and English reward models with good cross-model generalization
In-depth analysis of PPO inner workings and the PPO-max algorithm for stable training

method.summary: Trains English (LLaMA-7B) and Chinese (OpenChineseLLaMA-7B) reward models, then ablates PPO implementation tricks on a Chinese 7B SFT policy, monitoring perplexity, response length and KL; selected tricks form PPO-max, evaluated by human and GPT-4 win/tie/lose against SFT and ChatGPT.
method.task: RLHF / PPO for helpful and harmless alignment

datasets.name: HH-RLHF (English RM)
datasets.size: 160k pairs (118k helpful, 42k harmless) train; 1k test (about 0.7k helpful, 0.3k harmless); rest validation

datasets.name: Chinese preference data (annotator labelled)
datasets.size: 39k pairs (31k helpful, 8k harmless); train 24k helpful + 6k harmless; test 2.4k helpful + 0.6k harmless

datasets.name: C-Eval
datasets.size: about 13k multi-choice questions, 52 disciplines, four difficulty levels

models.name: OpenChineseLLaMA-7B (Chinese RM/SFT)
models.architecture: decoder-only; incremental Chinese pretraining of LLaMA-7B

models.name: Reward model
models.architecture: pretrained LM with unembedding removed, linear head giving scalar at last token; also LM loss on preferred response

models.name: Critic
models.init_from: reward model, then pretrained before PPO

training.objective: RM: pairwise log-sigmoid loss + beta_rm LM loss; policy: PPO-clip with token-level KL penalty (eta) on reward, optional PPO-ptx pretraining loss, MSE critic loss, GAE
training.lr_schedule: warmup over first 10% steps (RM and PPO)
training.batch_size: RM dynamic by tokens, max 128 min 4; PPO sampling batch 128, training batch 32 (policy and critic)
training.steps: RM fixed 1000 steps (~1.06 epoch); PPO 1000 steps in ablations, 10K steps for PPO-max (Fig 9)
training.regularisation: KL penalty (0.05 in Fig 7 experiment; 0.05/0.1/0.2 compared in Fig 15); reward normalisation and clipping; value-loss clipping; global gradient clipping; GAE lambda 0.9
training.hardware: machines with eight 80G A100 GPUs, 1TB RAM, 128 CPUs; ZeRO2 and gradient checkpointing

other.ppo_max_components: normalise and clip rewards using historical mean/variance; token-level KL penalty; critic initialised from RM and pretrained before PPO; global gradient clipping; small experience buffer; pretraining LM loss (PPO-ptx); value function loss clipping. Final numeric values for PPO-max are deferred to the released code

inference.samples: one response per test prompt per model

metrics.name: Preference win/tie/lose
metrics.definition: annotators or GPT-4 compare one response from each model per held-out prompt

metrics.name: Perplexity, KL to SFT, response length

eval.protocol: Human annotators (number not stated) and GPT-4 as judge, single response per prompt; number of eval prompts not stated; no seeds or significance tests.

results.claim: Policy constraints (token-level KL penalty) are the key to stable PPO in RLHF; PPO-max combines the selected tricks to give long stable training.
results.setup: 7B Chinese SFT policy, Chinese HH subset; stability judged by perplexity, response length, KL not reward
results.quote: We identify policy constraints being the key factor for the effective implementation of the PPO algorithm.

results.claim: Vanilla PPO suffers pattern collapse: reward and training loss converge smoothly while human/GPT-4 judgement disagrees; the policy cheats the RM with specific patterns, giving long-tail reward scores, longer responses and lower perplexity.
results.setup: Vanilla PPO, 1000 steps, 7B Chinese SFT, Fig 4
results.quote: However, we observe that the trained policy model has a tendency to cheat the reward model through specific patterns for anomalous higher scores.

results.claim: Collapsed model uniformly gives longer responses and lower perplexity.
results.quote: We simultaneously observe that the collapsed model uniformly delivers longer responses and exhibits lower perplexity for such generative patterns.

results.claim: KL-penalty coefficient used in the policy-constraint experiment (Fig 7) is 0.05; Anthropic's value was 0.001.
results.setup: Fig 7 KL penalty experiment; Fig 15 compares 0.05, 0.1, 0.2
results.note: Text calls it lambda; Eq 19 calls it eta. The paper does not state the final PPO-max coefficient in text (see code).
results.quote: Results with policy divergence penalty are illustrated in Figure 7 by setting lambda to 0.05

results.claim: Anthropic used a KL weight of 0.001 and reported no significant effect; this paper finds KL penalty critical.
results.quote: Anthropic [17] used a small weight to balance the ratio of reward and KL-penalty in PPO training (0.001)

results.claim: Reward model English: LLaMA-7B on 160k HH-RLHF pairs (118k helpful, 42k harmless); 1k test.
results.quote: We use 160k pairwise samples of the HH-RLHF dataset[17] which consists of 118k helpful and 42k harmless instances as training set.

results.claim: Reward model Chinese: OpenChineseLLaMA with 39k annotator-labelled pairs (31k helpful, 8k harmless); 30k train, 3k test.
results.quote: We hired professional annotators to manually label 39k pairwise samples including 31k helpful and 8k harmless samples.

results.claim: RM accuracy is only shown as curves (Fig 3), not numerically; Chinese RM accuracy is higher than English because Chinese pairs differ more; improvement slows after about 200 steps (~0.2 epoch).
results.quote: Besides, we find that the rate of improvement significantly slows down after 200 steps for both models, approximately equivalent to 0.2 epochs

results.claim: A 200-step RM gives similar accuracy to full training but PPO from it performs unsatisfactorily, so accuracy alone is insufficient to judge an RM.
results.quote: Thus, accuracy alone is insufficient as a criterion for the RM.

results.claim: RLHF vs SFT human evaluation: English harmless 62% win vs 5% lose (33% tie); English helpful 44% win vs 30% lose (26% tie).
results.setup: Human annotators, PPO-max RLHF vs SFT, held-out prompts, one response per prompt, comparator = SFT
results.note: Tie values 33% and 26% read from Fig 10a; 44% vs 30% quoted in text
results.quote: the RLHF model on the English dataset exhibits significant advantages on the Harmless held-out dataset, receiving a rating of 62% compared to 5% for the SFT model.

results.claim: Human evaluation Chinese: RLHF vs SFT harmless 39% win / 29% tie / 32% lose; helpful 46% / 23% / 31%.
results.setup: Human, PPO-max vs SFT (OpenChineseLLaMA SFT), read from Fig 10a bars (order zh harmless, zh helpful, en harmless, en helpful; win 39,46,62,44; tie 29,23,33,26; lose 32,31,5,30)
results.note: Values read from figure bars; each triple sums to 100
results.quote: Figure 10: Preference evaluations, compared RLHF models with SFT models in human evaluation (left) and GPT-4 evaluation (right).

results.claim: GPT-4 judge RLHF vs SFT: win/tie/lose zh harmless 25/60/15, zh helpful 52/17/31, en harmless 34/59/7, en helpful 43/23/34 (%).
results.setup: GPT-4 annotator, PPO-max vs SFT, read from Fig 10b
results.note: Values read from bars; GPT-4 yields more ties than humans on harmless.
results.quote: Figure 10: Preference evaluations, compared RLHF models with SFT models in human evaluation (left) and GPT-4 evaluation (right).

results.claim: Vs ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613) on harmless (GPT-4 judge), RLHF cut the defeat rate from 45% to 24% (English) and 37% to 29% (Chinese).
results.setup: GPT-4 judge, harmless prompts, ours vs ChatGPT; Fig 11 win/tie/lose: SFT zh 5/58/37, RLHF zh 6/65/29, SFT en 16/39/45, RLHF en 18/58/24
results.note: Win and tie values read from Fig 11; RLHF still lags ChatGPT
results.quote: the RLHF model trained on English text managed to decrease the defeat rate from 45% to 24%.

results.claim: PPO lowers C-Eval (Chinese NLU) scores; PPO-ptx (pretraining loss mixed in) alleviates the decline. Scores only in Fig 12 bars.
results.setup: Chinese RLHF 7B, C-Eval few-shot (~13k questions, 52 disciplines)
results.quote: The experimental results indicate a decrease in NLU capabilities after employing PPO.

results.claim: Policy initialised without SFT fails in PPO; critic init from RM vs SFT converges similarly; critic pre-training improves stability.
results.note: Exact quote text in paper: 'Initializing the critic model with a reward or SFT model will converge to similar results' (line break differs)
results.quote: Based on the experimental results, we believe the critic model pre-training helps to improve the training stability by providing better advantage estimation.

results.claim: Entropy bonus is highly sensitive: a 10% change in the clip threshold makes the run fail; KL penalty recommended instead.
results.quote: Delta is a hyperparameter that must be carefully tuned to prevent training collapse (our experiments fail with only a 10% change at this threshold).

results.claim: Importance sampling with KL penalty stabilises PPO further but compromises final policy performance.
results.quote: Experimental results indicate that this implementation further stabilizes PPO training, but compromises the final performance of the policy model.

results.claim: GAE lambda set to 0.9 in all other experiments; lambda 0 (TD) is numerically unstable, lambda 1 (MC) has larger variance.
results.quote: we set λ = 0.9 in all our other experiments

results.claim: Reward scaling alone does not prevent collapse, contradicting Engstrom et al.; reward normalise+clip, advantage clip and value clip conflict if mixed.
results.quote: we show that reward scaling doesn’t guide proper policy optimization

limits: Only 7B models studied; no scaling-law analysis of model or data size.
RM data is open English plus small self-built Chinese set; insufficient for comprehensive RM evaluation.
Evaluation relies on manual and GPT-4 judgement; no standard benchmarks except C-Eval.
Focus is stability not final performance; reward score cannot predict RLHF quality during training.
Exact PPO-max numeric hyperparameters, RM accuracy numbers, number of eval prompts and annotators are not stated in the text.
Ablations on a subset of Chinese data and not trained to optimum; single runs.

terms.definition: SFT models are over-optimized and exhibit highly biased behavior
the most suitable implementation we find for the language model
